extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and patent litigators (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and making rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 including rules on disqualification of prior art due to common ownership (35 U.S.C. 103(c)), double patenting practice, form paragraphs to use in 103 rejections, and special rules for biotechnological processes under 35 U.S.C. 103(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disqualification of subject matter as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant’s admission that subject matter was developed prior to applicant’s invention will not make the subject matter prior art to applicant if the subject matter qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or 102(g), or (for applications filed on or after November 29, 1999) 35 U.S.C. 102(e), and if the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Fout as contrast where an admission was used as prior art. Emphasizes that disqualification applies only when the reference is available solely under the identified subsections and common ownership at time invention was made is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for establishing disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) is intended to be placed and reside upon the person or persons urging that the subject matter is disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a patent applicant urging disqualification must establish common ownership. The patentee in litigation likewise bears the burden. It is inappropriate to place the burden on the examiner or litigation defendant because evidence of common ownership may not be available to them but should be readily available to applicant/patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of double patenting rejections in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the Commissioner has reinstituted in appropriate circumstances the practice of rejecting claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities on the grounds of double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by filing terminal disclaimers. This prevents improper extension of patent protection while permitting legitimate benefits to inventors/assignees. See MPEP § 804 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating common ownership/failure to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP provides concrete examples (e.g., Parent owns 100% of Subsidiaries A and B → commonly owned; Parent owns 100% of A and 90% of B → inventions are not commonly owned; same person owning subject matter and invention may license without creating prior art; government inventors retaining certain rights may preclude common ownership; joint venture facts determine common ownership).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual analysis and evidence to determine whether common ownership existed at the time the later invention was made. Example 5: joint venture employees assigning to C — common ownership depends on who actually owned earlier invention at that time. Example 6: fractional ownership allocations (40%/60% vs 60%/40%) can result in common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal requirement for common ownership (time of invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common ownership must be shown to exist at the time the later invention was made; a statement of present common ownership is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention is 'made' when conception is complete (cases cited). Pfaff v. Wells standard invoked: invention must be 'ready for patenting' (e.g., drawings or descriptions sufficiently specific to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention). Common ownership may be established irrespective of where the invention was made (U.S. or abroad) for purposes of disqualification under 102/103, though other statutes (35 U.S.C. 104) continue to apply in other proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient statement by applicant/attorney to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and references will be considered to be owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person at the time the invention was made if the applicant(s) or an attorney or agent of record makes a statement to that effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement is sufficient because of the applicant/representative's obligation of candor and good faith. The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on separate paper or labeled section) so the examiner quickly notices it. Applicants may but are not required to submit additional evidence (assignments, affidavits/declarations, court decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence the applicant may submit to establish common ownership (A–D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence that may be submitted includes: (A) reference to assignments recorded in the USPTO conveying entire rights to the same person(s) or organization(s); (B) copies of unrecorded assignments filed in each application; (C) an affidavit or declaration by the common owner stating common ownership facts and explaining belief in common ownership; (D) other evidence establishing common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner has independent evidence raising material doubt about applicant's representation, the examiner may require objective evidence of common ownership of, or the existence of an obligation to assign, the application and applied reference as of the date of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership is not established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application file does not establish common ownership at the time the invention was made, the examiner will assume the applications and patents are not commonly owned and will examine the application on all grounds other than any conflict arising from a possible 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) and/or (g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner should consider the applicability of references under 103 based on 102(e),(f),(g), including provisional rejections under 102(e)/103, and apply the best references against the claimed invention by rejections under 102 and 103 until a statement of common ownership is made. For apps filed on/after Nov 29, 1999, anticipate a statement that may disqualify a 102(e) reference; if such statement is filed in reply and claims not amended, the examiner may not make the next Office action final if a new rejection is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership is established (apps filed on/after Nov 29, 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the file establishes that the application and any reference were owned by, or subject to an obligation/assignment to, the same person at the time the invention was made, the examiner will examine the applications as to all grounds except 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) and (g) as they apply through 35 U.S.C. 103, and will examine for double patenting and invite the applicant to file a terminal disclaimer if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes examining provisional rejections under 102(e)/103 as appropriate and treating double patenting issues (statutory and nonstatutory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership is established (apps filed prior to Nov 29, 1999)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed prior to Nov 29, 1999, where common ownership is established, the examiner will examine as to all grounds except 35 U.S.C. 102(f) and (g) as they apply through 103; examine for double patenting (statutory and nonstatutory) and make provisional 102(e)/103 rejections as appropriate; invite terminal disclaimer; and permit affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 or 1.132 where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure of an earlier filed application that issues as a patent continues to be prior art under 102(e) against a later-filed application of another inventor even though both were commonly owned at the time the later invention was made (see MPEP § 706.02(l)(1)). Specific remediation procedures (terminal disclaimer, affidavits under 1.131/1.132) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting rejection and how to overcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the ground of double patenting, including in cases where later-filed application claims 35 U.S.C. 120 benefit to the earlier application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections prevent an organization from obtaining multiple patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. They can be overcome in certain circumstances by disclaiming, pursuant to 37 CFR 1.321, the terminal portion of the term of the later patent and including a provision that the patent shall be enforceable only during the period of common ownership with the application/patent that formed the basis for the rejection. See MPEP §§ 804, 804.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraph 7.20 — Statement of Statutory Basis, 35 U.S.C. 103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.20 quotes 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and forms the basis for all obviousness rejections in Office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute is required in first actions on the merits employing 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and in final rejections. Where the statute is applied but not cited, use paragraph 7.103. This form paragraph must precede certain form paragraphs (7.20.01–7.22) when the statute is cited. Use this paragraph only once in a given Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.20.01 — apps filed prior to Nov 29, 1999 using art disqualified under 102(f) or (g)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant has provided evidence showing the invention was owned by, or subject to assignment to, the same entity as the applied art at the time the invention was made, identify the commonly owned applied art and state that it is disqualified as prior art through 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g) in any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that the applied art may still qualify under another subsection of 35 U.S.C. 102 and thus might not be disqualified; advise on how applicant may overcome the applied art (37 CFR 1.132 antedating, 1.131). Must be included following 7.20 in actions containing rejections under 103(a) using art disqualified under 103(c) using 102(f)/(g) for pre-Nov 29, 1999 apps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.20.03 — apps filed on/after Nov 29, 1999 using art disqualified under 102(e), (f) or (g)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications filed on or after Nov 29, 1999, when applicant has provided evidence of common ownership, identify the commonly owned applied art and state that it is disqualified as prior art through 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) in any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that the applied art might additionally qualify under another subsection of 102 and thus not be disqualified. Applicant may overcome the applied art by 37 CFR 1.132 showing derivation or by 1.131 antedating. Must be used in appropriate post-Nov 29, 1999 cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.20.02 — Joint inventors; common ownership presumed
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application names joint inventors, the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time inventions covered therein were made absent evidence to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out inventor and invention dates for any claim not commonly owned so the examiner may consider applicability of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential 102(e),(f),(g) prior art. This paragraph must be used in all applications with joint inventors unless claims are clearly restricted to a single claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.21 and related form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections (¶ 7.21, 7.21.01, 7.21.02, 7.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: ¶ 7.21: Generic rejection form for claims under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over identified art; must be followed by an explanation applying the Graham v. Deere test. ¶ 7.21.01: Provisional rejection under 103(a) based on copending application with common assignee or at least one common inventor (anticipation if copending app later patents). ¶ 7.21.02: Rejection under 103(a) where applied reference has a common assignee or at least one common inventor, and ways to overcome. ¶ 7.22: Rejection under 103(a) 'further in view of' another reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each paragraph has Examiner Notes specifying when to use, required follow-ups (e.g., Graham analysis), how to fill bracketed insertions (e.g., identify common assignee/inventor), and how such rejections may be overcome (37 CFR 1.131, 1.132, 1.130 plus terminal disclaimer for certain cases). Use 7.21.01 for provisional rejections where appropriate; do not use 7.21.01 for post-Nov 29, 1999 applications when common ownership is established per §706.02(l)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. Deere test factors for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual inquiries set forth in Graham v. John Deere Co. used to establish a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a): (1) Determining the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanation applying the Graham test must follow form paragraphs that assert a 103(a) rejection. Paragraph 7.23 may be used in response to an argument invoking Graham v. Deere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of combined 102/103 form paragraph 7.27
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 7.27 allows a claim to be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(x) as anticipated or alternatively under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as obvious over a cited reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paragraph is NOT intended for routine use; a single rejection under either 102 or 103 should be made whenever possible. Provides examples of circumstances where combined paragraph may be appropriate (e.g., claim interpretation disputes, inherent properties, genus/species issues, means-plus-function uncertainties, overlapping ranges). A full explanation applying Graham must follow, and this paragraph must be preceded by other specified form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) special rules for biotechnological processes
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(b) provides that, notwithstanding subsection (a), a biotechnological process using or resulting in a composition of matter novel under 102 and nonobvious under 103(a) shall be considered nonobvious if (1) claims to the process and composition are in the same application or in separate applications having the same effective filing date, and (2) the composition and the process at the time invented were owned by or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional requirements: (A) patent on process must also contain claims to composition used or made by the process or, if composition is in another patent, patents must expire on same date; (B) definition of 'biotechnological process' enumerated (genetically altering organisms to express/inhibit sequences or express specific physiological characteristics; cell fusion procedures yielding cell lines expressing specific proteins; methods of using products produced by such processes); (C) timely election to proceed under 103(b) via petition under 37 CFR 1.182 must be made, normally no later than earlier of payment of issue fee or filing of an appeal brief; (D) for pending apps where issue fee paid prior to specific dates, timeliness may be satisfied by 37 CFR 1.312(b) conditions; (E) if patent issued without election due to error without deceptive intent, reissue may be filed to permit consideration of process claims qualifying for 103(b) treatment. See MPEP § 2116.01 and cited Federal Circuit decisions.
